newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan won't alter liquor tax changes for now -- MOF.
newsitem.headline: Japan won't alter liquor tax changes for now -- MOF.

text.p: Japan"s Finance Ministry will not alter bills submitted to parliament to correct the disparity between domestic and foreign liquor taxes regardless of the outcome of outstanding WTO arbitration, a ministry official said on Friday.
"Regardless of WTO (World Trade Organisation) arbitration, we hope to have the bills debated as they are now," the official said.
He added that if changes need to be made, they could be submitted at later sessions of parliament.
The United States had asked for arbitration by the WTO after the two nations failed to agree on the length of the period in which the disparity should be corrected.
The ruling was expected later on Friday.

The WTO, ruling on a complaint by the European Union, the United States and Canada, decided in November 1996 that Japan taxes imported liquor unfairly compared with domestic spirits. It called for revisions to be made within 15 months, in accordance with WTO procedures.

Japan proposed in December a plan to correct the disparity by raising taxes on domestic liquor known as "shochu" while lowering those for whiskey and other spirits over a five-year period starting October 1997.
The bills to implement these changes have been submitted to the current session of parliament which ends in June.
Japan and the European Union signed a formal agreement in January, but the United States and Japan failed to reach an agreement and the issue was put to WTO arbitration.

Japanese media reports said that the WTO arbitrator has urged Japan to reduce the transition phase to 15 months, effectively requiring Japan to complete the process by February 1, 1998. The United States wanted a five-month transition.
Industry sources said Japan can resume bilateral negotiations with the United States for compensatory measures so it would be able to carry out its tax revisions as planned.

However, media reports said that since the two sides failed to reach an agreement before Japan had offered speedier tariff cuts for bourbon whiskey, Washington may take retaliatory steps against Tokyo as allowed under WTO rules.
